The train had been stuck outside Itarsi for two hours, the fan had died, and Tejas and Hrithik were down to their last packet of chips and a pack of cards. They played a simple game: shuffle, turn one card, bet two chips on red or black, put it back, shuffle again.
Black came seven times in a row. Tejas pushed his whole pile forward. "Red now. Has to be. Seven blacks, the deck owes me."
"We reshuffle every time, Tejas," said Hrithik. "The deck's forgotten."
"Doesn't matter. Streaks break."
Black.
Tejas groaned and flopped back against the window. Hrithik, generous in the heat, gave him back three chips. "For the next bet. Think first."
Outside, the train finally lurched forward.

qa.q: What were Tejas and Hrithik betting on each card?
qa.a: They bet two chips on red or black.

qa.q: Why did Tejas push his whole pile forward after seven blacks?
qa.a: He felt sure a red was owed after such a long run, so betting everything felt safe and clever. 😅

qa.q: What could Tejas do before the next bet, as Hrithik's 'Think first' suggests?
qa.a: Tejas could remind himself the deck is reshuffled each time, so seven blacks tell him nothing, and bet small or not at all.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik react so differently to the seven blacks?
qa.a: Hrithik focuses on the reshuffle rather than the streak, so the run doesn't feel meaningful and there's no urge to bet it all.

grounding: A teen on a stalled train bets all his chips that red must come after seven blacks, though the deck is reshuffled each time.

In their Hyderabad housing colony, everyone followed the Kukatpally Kings, who had lost six matches straight in the inter-colony league. On the parapet outside Block B, Yusuf was certain.
"Seventh one they win. Six losses in a row, it has to turn. Bet you a week of samosas."
Abhinav looked up from his phone. "Their best bowler's injured. Their keeper moved to Pune. What's going to turn?"
"The luck," said Yusuf. "Streaks don't last forever."
"Even a coin doesn't owe you a head after six tails."
On Sunday evening the Kings lost by forty runs. On Monday morning Yusuf handed over the first samosa, then started on the next bet: "Eighth match, surely..."
Abhinav held up a hand. "No more bets, bhai."

qa.a: They had lost six matches straight.

qa.q: What makes 'Streaks don't last forever' feel convincing to Yusuf?
qa.a: Yusuf feels hopeful and certain because after six losses a win seems overdue, as though luck keeps an account that has to balance.

qa.q: When Yusuf started on the eighth-match bet, what choice did Abhinav make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Abhinav stopped the betting with "No more bets, bhai", ending the chase before Yusuf lost more samosas on the same idea.

qa.q: How might the Kings' players see Yusuf's certainty?
qa.a: They know they have lost their best bowler and keeper, so they might find it odd that Yusuf expects a win from luck rather than from the team.

grounding: A teen bets a week of samosas that a losing colony team must win after six losses.

I'm Reena, and in Class 10 I made a bet I still get teased about. Our house, Blue, had lost seven football matches in a row in the inter-house league. Seven! I told Yusuf, "Law of averages. Blue wins the eighth. It's due."
Yusuf said the eighth match didn't know about the other seven. I said a streak that long had to break, and I bet him a week of carrying his school bag up four floors.
Blue lost 3–0. Our goalkeeper had a sprained wrist, and Red had two players from the district team. The old losses meant nothing; only who was on the field that day did.
I carried that bag for five days. On day three Yusuf grinned. "Bet Blue wins the ninth?" I said no. I had finally noticed I'd been counting the wrong thing.

qa.q: What did Reena bet Yusuf?
qa.a: A week of carrying Yusuf's school bag up four floors.

qa.q: How did Reena feel about the eighth match, and why?
qa.a: Reena felt confident that Blue was due to win, because seven losses seemed too long a run, confident enough to bet a week of carrying Yusuf's bag.

qa.q: What turning point came for Reena, and what was a better way to judge the next match?
qa.a: Turning down Yusuf's bet on the ninth match; looking at who was actually on the field, like the injured goalkeeper, says far more than the old streak.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see the week of bag carrying?
qa.a: Yusuf probably enjoys winning and teasing, but the offer on day three also looks like a test of whether Reena has learned anything.

grounding: It shows a teenager betting friendly stakes that a team is due to win after a long losing run, then noticing each match stands on its own.

Warden's note, girls' hostel, Friday (Farida)
Around nine I found five Class 11 girls on the common-room floor with a pack of cards. Each round someone shuffled the full deck and cut one card. The ace of spades had not come up in fifteen cuts, and Deepika had bet her weekend chocolate stash against Mansi's that it would come next.
"Fifteen cuts! It has to show up now," Deepika said. With every miss she added another bar.
I sat down and asked whether a freshly shuffled deck could know what was cut before. "No," she said, "but it's been so long." We cut twenty more times together and wrote each card down. The ace came once, at cut seventeen. She looked at the list for a long time.
Next: chocolates returned to their owners; I'll ask the maths teacher to run the counting game at study hour.

qa.q: How many cuts had passed without the ace of spades when Deepika made her bet?
qa.a: Fifteen cuts.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel as the ace keeps not coming, and what shows it?
qa.a: Deepika feels more and more eager and certain the ace is overdue, saying "It has to show up now" and adding another bar with every miss.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make that could change Deepika's thinking?
qa.a: Farida asked whether a freshly shuffled deck could remember past cuts and then counted twenty cuts together, letting the written list show that misses don't bring the ace any sooner.

qa.q: How might Mansi feel as Deepika keeps raising the bet?
qa.a: Mansi might enjoy the growing pile at first, but could grow uneasy watching a friend lose more and more on each miss.

grounding: It shows a teenager betting friendly stakes that a card must turn up after a long run of misses, though each shuffled cut has no memory.

passage: On the train home from school in Prague, Vera and Noa played cards for squares of chocolate. Vera had drawn no aces for nine rounds. "The next one's an ace," she said. "Nine rounds without. "You know the deck gets shuffled every time, right? It forgets." Vera frowned at the empty chocolate wrapper. "Then why does it feel like it owes me?" "Because you remember the nine rounds," Noa said. "The cards don't."

Dear Tushar,
You'll laugh. Remember our family's monsoon cricket pool, where everyone puts in ten rupees and picks a team? This year I picked the Rhinos, who had lost eight matches in a row. My reasoning was genius: they HAD to win soon. Eight losses meant a win was due. Dadu said, "Beta, they lost eight because their captain retired," but I didn't listen. I even talked Mishti into picking them with me.
They lost the next three. Mishti hasn't forgiven me.
When I told my maths teacher, she said each match is decided by the players on the day, not by what happened before. Streaks feel like they must end, she said, but they don't owe anybody anything.
Lesson learned. Next year I'm picking by who's actually playing.
Usha

qa.q: Why did the Rhinos lose eight, according to Dadu?
qa.a: Because their captain retired.

qa.q: Why was Usha sure the Rhinos would win soon?
qa.a: Usha felt confident that eight losses meant a win was due, as if the streak had to balance out.

qa.q: What does Usha plan for next year, and why is it better?
qa.a: Picking by who is actually playing, because matches depend on the players on the day, not on past streaks.

qa.q: How does Mishti feel about the pool?
qa.a: Mishti hasn't forgiven Usha for talking her into the Rhinos, so she is probably annoyed.

grounding: A teenager writes about betting a small family stake on a team because a win seemed due after a long losing run.

passage: Sabina, I lost the samosa bet, and I want to explain before you laugh. Okay, laugh a little. So, I'm Madhuri, and our house team, Blue House, had lost six inter-house football matches in a row. Six! So I thought, this is it. The seventh has to be a win. It's due. I told the whole class, and I bet the girl next to me a samosa every day for a week. We lost 3–0. And instead of learning, what did I do? I said, the eighth is definitely due, and I doubled it. Two samosas. We lost again. Then our sports teacher heard me and said, "Each match is new, Madhuri. The team doesn't owe you a win because they lost before." I owe fourteen samosas now. I'm not betting again.

passage: Tanvir beta, you think your team must win on Sunday because they've lost five in a row? Let your Zainab Nani tell you about the summer of 1985 in Hyderabad. I was fifteen, and cricket-mad. Our local club had lost eight matches straight. I was so sure the ninth would be a win that I bet my cousin I would do all her chores for a week if they lost. They lost. The lights of the Hyderabad wedding hall were still on at midnight, and the cousins had taken over a corner with a pack of cards and a bowl of toffees for stakes.
Wasim was playing Usha at a simple game: draw one card from the full pack; a king wins a toffee. After every draw, Usha pushed the card back in and shuffled. Nine draws now, and no king.
"King next," Wasim said, pushing all six of his toffees into the middle. "Nine draws, no king. It's coming. It has to."
"You said that four draws ago," Usha said.
"Which makes it even more certain now."
Usha shuffled and turned the top card. A seven of clubs.
Wasim slapped the carpet. "This deck is rigged."
"It's Chachi's deck," Usha said, sweeping the toffees toward herself. "I shuffle it back every time. It has no clue what came out before."

qa.q: How many draws had passed without a king?
qa.a: Nine draws had passed with no king.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he pushed all his toffees in?
qa.a: Wasim felt certain and excited, believing a king was owed after nine misses.

qa.q: What would help Wasim in the next round?
qa.a: Wasim could remember that every card goes back and is shuffled, so a king has the same chance on each draw, and not stake everything on a 'due' king.

qa.q: How does Usha see Wasim's claim that the deck is rigged?
qa.a: Usha finds it silly and calmly explains that shuffling each card back means the deck has no memory.
